One-sentence judgment: cabinetmakers and bench carpenters are not about "throwing a cabinet together"; they measure and lay out lumber to drawings, cut and shape it, work the joints, and assemble cabinets, fixtures, and fine furniture, while being responsible for dimensional fit, material matching, and surface preparation. O*NET classifies this occupation as Job Zone 1-2 (little to some preparation needed, SVP below 6.0), does not mark it Bright Outlook, and gives an interest code of RC. The core boundary: you may operate woodworking machines such as saws, jointers, and mortisers to drawings, assemble parts, install hardware, and do final inspection; but you may not keep working when guards are missing or equipment is abnormal, may not change structural load-bearing or installation plans on your own, and may not claim the decisions on equipment shutdown and restart or on on-site installation handover as your own.

Signals to keep exploring: you can stand for long periods and use hand and power tools steadily; you are willing to check dimensions and fit repeatedly against the same drawing; you can accept dust, noise, and repetitive motion and consistently wear protective equipment; you are willing to stop the machine and report first when you notice an abnormality in a saw blade, guard, or drive component; and you accept a daily routine centered on shop machining, assembly, and dimensional records.

Conditions for pausing major investment first: you have not yet completed one full closed loop from reading drawings and laying out, cutting and shaping, joint work, and hardware assembly through dimensional verification and surface-preparation prep; or you are unwilling to follow equipment guarding and dust-and-noise-control requirements and just want to work "by feel" without looking at drawings and tolerances; also, do not treat having done small wood projects at home as proof that you can operate woodworking machines independently.

Education, credentials, and authorization must be checked separately: O*NET classifies this occupation as Job Zone 1-2 (little to some preparation needed, SVP below 6.0); a high school diploma or equivalent (GED) is usually required, some positions do not require it, and on-the-job training ranges from a few days to a year. In the United States, job requirements are set by employers and the rules of the state; in mainland China, the Occupational Classification Code of the People's Republic of China (2022 edition) has no one-to-one sub-category matching this entry, and the related duties may fall under wood product machining, furniture manufacturing, and architectural woodwork installation positions, so they must be judged by the actual duties of the position, and it is made clear that the Chinese page language does not constitute a China-equivalent occupation or wage mapping. Credentials, equipment operating authorization, the right to stop a machine, and the right to hand over an installation are four different things and cannot substitute for one another.

In one sentence: this is a role that turns drawings into dimensionally accurate, solidly assembled wood products; the outputs are cabinets and furniture parts machined and assembled to specification, hardware installed in place, dimensional and fit verification records, and surface preparation and handover notes; it is not the final approving role for structural design and installation plans, nor does it replace the division of responsibility for equipment safety and on-site work. This page does not publish occupation-level wage figures for mainland China, and it makes clear that the Chinese page language does not constitute a China-equivalent occupation or wage mapping.

The work of this occupation falls into three categories: first, machining and shaping (measuring and laying out to drawings, cutting and shaping, fitting joints with hand tools, setting up and operating woodworking machines, drilling); second, assembly and hardware (assembling parts and subassemblies into complete units, reinforcing joints, installing hardware such as hinges and slides, sanding and final inspection touch-up); third, quality and delivery (verifying dimensions and fit, matching materials by color and grain, preparing for surface finishing, repairing and modifying, estimating materials and checking customer specifications). All three share the same chain built around drawings, tolerances, and fit.
Machining and shaping

Read drawings and measure out → mark dimensions and tolerances → cut lumber and true the joints → set up and operate woodworking machines to shape → drill for screws or dowels → recheck dimensions, then move to assembly.
Assembly and hardware

Match parts and subassemblies → apply glue and position → assemble into a complete unit → reinforce joints → install hardware such as hinges and slides → sand and do final inspection touch-up and record.

Editorial collaboration note: checking gauges and drawings, reporting abnormalities, and handover should follow the position's procedures; when missing guards or a hazard is found, stop, report, and prevent further use under the applicable procedures; when maintenance carries a risk of unexpected start-up or energy release, it is handled by appropriate personnel under hazardous-energy isolation, verification, and restoration procedures. Pressing a stop button does not equal isolation, and this text grants no authority to repair or restart.

This occupation mainly manufactures and assembles wood products, while construction carpenters lean more toward on-site structure and installation; real positions can overlap, and helpers or installers are not uniformly excluded from independent tasks.
Core purpose

Turn drawings and customer specifications into wood products that are dimensionally accurate, solidly assembled, and consistent in appearance: control fit through measuring, layout, and joint fitting; ensure strength through assembly and reinforcement; ensure appearance through material matching and surface-preparation prep.
Main objects and basis

The objects are lumber and wood substitute panels, drawings and customer specifications, hand tools such as planes, chisels, and rasps, woodworking machines such as power saws, jointers, and mortisers, glue, dowels, and fasteners, hardware such as hinges, pulls, and slides, and sandpaper, steel wool, and finishing materials; the basis is drawing and tolerance requirements, material and grain matching rules, joint and assembly process requirements, equipment operating and guarding requirements, dust and noise protection requirements, and the inspecting and handover procedures of the employing company.
Core process

Reading drawings and laying out, cutting and shaping, joint fitting, drilling, assembly and reinforcement, hardware installation, dimensional and fit verification, sanding and final inspection, surface preparation, and stopping the machine and reporting abnormalities and handover.
Main outputs

Cabinets, fixtures, and fine furniture parts and units machined and assembled to specification, hardware installed in place, dimensional and fit verification records, material matching and material estimation records, surface preparation and final inspection touch-up records, and handover notes.
Accountable party

Editorial check of the responsibility interfaces for design, process, inspection, and equipment management; the specific division of labor and signing authority follow the target position's system and are not determined automatically by the occupation name.
Authority and approval

Article 28 of China's Work Safety Law provides that a person may take up the post only after passing training, with records kept; Article 30 requires separately checking the catalog and qualifications for special operations, which does not imply that all woodworkers fall under special operations; the rights under Articles 54—55 to refuse violations and to stop/evacuate when personal safety is directly endangered do not depend on internal authorization. Equipment operation and maintenance isolation and restoration must be checked against the actual system separately; this round did not comprehensively check individual permits, local requirements, or product standards.
Conclusion boundaries

Dimensional and fit records describe "what state machining and assembly are in under the given drawings, tolerances, materials, and equipment conditions"; they are not a structural safety conclusion and do not replace the approval of design and installation plans, and they are updated as drawing revisions, material batches, and equipment conditions change; when citing them, state the drawing revision and batch as well.

Before starting, check at least six items: job duties (custom machining, batch production, or on-site installation support), equipment operating authorization and training arrangements, the scope of responsibility for drawings and tolerances, dust and noise protection measures, working conditions for materials and surface finishing, and whether you are responsible for material estimation and communicating customer specifications.
Occupation scope

Interest RC: R100/C40/A25/I18/E4/S2; the specific-field scores of construction carpentry 99 and physical/manual work 80 are a separate set of measures, are not counted as realistic-type sub-scores, and are not a personal pass line. The O*NET industry distribution is manufacturing 78% and other 22% (including construction), which differs from the wage industry classification, and wages cannot be inferred from the proportions. A one-to-one Chinese occupation code was not established this round.
Education and training paths

U.S. survey of entry-level education requirements: 76% high school or equivalent, 21% less than high school, 3% some college, no degree; this is a survey, not the education composition of incumbents. For this BLS sub-category the typical entry-level education is high school/equivalent, related experience None, and mid-term OJT. Zone1—2, from a few days to a year, is the broad preparation level; the OOH notes that entry tasks for wood products workers sometimes take under a month, with proficiency taking months to more than a year, and actual positions must be checked separately.
Methods and tools

Safety and work permits

99% stand continuously or almost continuously, 95% use their hands continuously; 40% are exposed daily to the risk of minor burns, cuts, bites, or stings — this is not 40% being injured every day. Wood dust can harm the skin and respiratory system; noise requires assessment and control. The U.S. OSHA eTool emphasizes local exhaust ventilation and its maintenance and control of noise at the source and along the transmission path, with hearing protection as the last line of defense; measures are set based on the applicable assessment, and job rotation does not replace engineering controls.
Training and regulatory requirements

Article 28 of China's Work Safety Law provides that a person may take up the post only after passing training, with records kept; Article 30 requires separately checking the catalog and qualifications for special operations, which does not imply that all woodworkers fall under special operations; the rights under Articles 54—55 to refuse violations and to stop/evacuate when personal safety is directly endangered do not depend on internal authorization. Equipment operation and maintenance isolation and restoration must be checked against the actual system separately; this round did not comprehensively check individual permits, local requirements, or product standards. In the United States, OSHA1910.213 guarding and control of hazardous energy during servicing, and the maintenance isolation rules applicable under 1910.147, are each checked separately and not applied across jurisdictions.
Pay and hours

96% have a regular work schedule and 27% work more than 40 hours per week; these are different survey items and do not prove that every shop handling rush orders necessarily works overtime. Shifts, piece rates, and delivery deadlines should be checked in writing for the position.

Cabinetmakers and bench carpenters (O*NET-SOC 51-7011.00) cut, shape, and assemble wooden articles, or set up and operate a variety of woodworking machines (such as power saws, jointers, and mortisers) to surface, cut, or shape lumber, or fabricate parts for wood products. Daily work includes: measuring and laying out on paper or on lumber and marking dimensions to drawings; cutting lumber to the correct size and truing joints with hand tools (planes, chisels, rasps) so they fit tightly; setting up and operating machines such as power saws, jointers, mortisers, tenoners, and shapers to cut and shape; drilling for screws or dowels; using glue, dowels, nails, screws, or clamps to assemble parts and subassemblies into complete units; reinforcing joints with nails or other fasteners; installing hardware such as hinges, pulls, catches, and drawer slides; matching materials by color, grain, and species while watching for features such as knots; verifying dimensions and checking quality and fit against specifications; sanding and truing joints and doing final inspection touch-up; preparing for surface finishing; repairing or modifying wooden furniture, cabinets, fixtures, and paneling; they may also use drafting software to design furniture, write programs for machines, estimate the quantity and cost of materials needed, and discuss project specifications with customers. It carries responsibility for dimensional fit, solid assembly, and surface-preparation prep, but does not replace responsibility for structural design approval, equipment safety management, or on-site installation plans.

O*NET occupation identity and tasks: O*NET-SOC 51-7011.00 Cabinetmakers and Bench Carpenters, page updated in 2026, classified as Job Zone 1-2 (little to some preparation needed, SVP below 6.0), not marked Bright Outlook. The official duties are "Cut, shape, and assemble wooden articles or set up and operate a variety of woodworking machines, such as power saws, jointers, and mortisers to surface, cut, or shape lumber or to fabricate parts for wood products."; the page lists 20 tasks (14 core + 6 supplementary); the core tasks cover verifying dimensions and fit against specifications (85), producing or assembling parts such as cabinets and fine furniture (84), sanding and truing surfaces and joints to prepare for finishing (83), measuring and laying out to drawings (83), cutting and truing joints (83), matching materials by color and grain (83), setting up and operating woodworking machines (82), determining specifications and processes from drawings (81), drilling (80), assembling parts and subassemblies (80), reinforcing joints (79), installing hardware (79), final inspection touch-up (77), and repair and modification (72); supplementary tasks include designing furniture with drafting software (84), writing programs for machines (84), spraying protective or decorative finishes (73), discussing and drawing up detailed specifications with customers (70), estimating material quantities and costs (69), and applying surface materials (58).

U.S. wages (exact scope for this occupation): the BLS 2025 OEWS data shown by O*NET give this occupation (51-7011.00) a national median annual wage of $46,680 and a median hourly wage of $22.44; the 10th, 25th, 75th, and 90th percentiles for annual wages are $35,650, $38,830, $55,760, and $63,720, and the 10th, 25th, 75th, and 90th percentiles for hourly wages are $17.14, $18.67, $26.81, and $30.64. The median means that half of the workers earn above it and half below; it is not an entry-level wage or a starting-salary promise, and percentile figures cannot be treated as an individual job offer.

The national wage distribution for this occupation in China is still insufficient evidence; the NBS2025 figures of 113594 yuan/year for urban non-private manufacturing units and 76055 yuan/year for private units are pre-tax annual average industry background, mixing multiple occupations, and match a manufacturing scenario rather than an exact occupation wage.

U.S. BLS table 1.2 for this occupation 51-7011: 81800 in 2025 → 79400 in 2035, a net change of -2400 and a change of -2.9% (O*NET rounds to -3%, Decline), with an average of 6900 openings per year over 2025—2035; openings are not net growth and do not predict an individual's job. paragraphs: This page compares cabinetmakers and bench carpenters with five adjacent directions on the same set of dimensions: career direction, core work and outputs, key differences, and which direction each preference is better suited to. Adjacent directions are described according to their own official occupation descriptions and do not mean the job titles are interchangeable.

Evidence note: the career direction and core outputs are based on O*NET 51-7011.00 and the official descriptions of the adjacent entries (U.S. scope); equipment operating authorization, responsibility for drawings and tolerances, and inspection and stop-work authority must be verified separately for each company and jurisdiction, and this page does not present any direction as a shortcut for changing careers.

The table below compares the differences in duties and outputs between cabinetmakers and bench carpenters and the adjacent directions; the basis for judging is the main outputs, what the work is accountable for, and the required authorization, not how similar the job titles are.

Carpenters work at the construction site, dealing with structural dimensions, support, and installation conditions, and their output is building components; this occupation machines and assembles in the shop to drawings, dealing with tolerances and fit, and its output is deliverable wood product parts and units.
If you would rather build and install at a construction site, look first at the carpenters direction; if you would rather machine and assemble in a shop to drawings, look first at this occupation.
Build and install wooden structures, framing, and finish components at the construction site, with output centered on on-site structures and installation quality.
Carpenters

Furniture finishers focus on surface finishing and appearance and take on almost no structural machining or assembly; this occupation centers on dimensions, joints, and assembly, with surface-preparation prep being only one step before delivery.
If you would rather do finishing and appearance work, look first at the furniture finishers direction; if you would rather do machining and assembly, look first at this occupation.
Responsible for the surface finishing, coloring, and touching up of wood products, with output centered on surface appearance and coating quality.
Furniture Finishers

Sheet metal workers work with sheet metal, and their processes involve shearing, bending, and seaming, with material properties different from lumber; this occupation works with lumber and wood-based panels, and its processes center on cutting, joinery, joint fitting, and glued assembly.
If you would rather machine sheet metal components, look first at the sheet metal workers direction; if you would rather machine lumber and do joint assembly, look first at this occupation.
Make and install ventilation, roofing, and exterior components out of sheet metal, with output centered on metal components.
Sheet Metal Workers

Boilermakers face high pressure-containment and welding qualification requirements, and their responsibility lies in structural strength and weld quality; this occupation faces dimensional tolerances and assembly fit, and its responsibility lies in fit precision and appearance consistency.

If you would rather do pressure containment and large metal structures, look first at the boilermakers direction; if you would rather do wood product machining and assembly, look first at this occupation.
Fabricate and install pressure vessels and large metal structures, with output centered on pressure- and load-bearing structures.
Boilermakers

Carpenter helpers mainly assist and move materials and do not make independent machining and inspection conclusions; this occupation independently completes drawing reading and layout, machining, assembly, and dimensional verification and keeps records.

If you would rather start with support work and site preparation, look first at the carpenter helpers direction; if you are willing to independently take on machining and inspection responsibility, look first at this occupation.
Move materials, clean up the site, and provide support under the direction of others, with output centered on support work and site preparation.
Helpers--Carpenters

That assembler occupation works to aviation standards, and its inspection records and airworthiness requirements are far stricter than those for ordinary wood products; this occupation works to the drawings and tolerances for furniture and architectural woodwork, and is accountable for fit precision and appearance.

If you would rather assemble structures to aviation standards, look first at the aircraft structure assembly direction; if you would rather do wood product machining and assembly, look first at this occupation.
Assemble airframe structures and systems to aviation standards, with output centered on aviation assembly and airworthiness records.
Aircraft Structure, Surfaces, Rigging, and Systems Assemblers

Conclusion: the choice of direction is based on the main outputs, what the work is accountable for, and the required authorization, not on how similar the names are; once the direction is set, check the target position item by item for equipment operating authorization, the scope of responsibility for drawings and tolerances, dust and noise protection measures, and shift and overtime arrangements, and keep written confirmation.

entries.answer: Measure and lay out on paper or on lumber and mark dimensions to drawings, cut lumber and true joints with hand tools, set up and operate woodworking machines such as power saws, jointers, mortisers, and shapers to cut and shape, drill for screws or dowels, apply glue and position and assemble parts and subassemblies into complete units, reinforce joints with fasteners, install hardware such as hinges, pulls, catches, and drawer slides, match materials by color and grain, verify dimensions, quality, and fit against specifications, sand and do final inspection touch-up and prepare for surface finishing, and also repair or modify wooden furniture and fixtures.
entries.question: What do cabinetmakers and bench carpenters do every day?

entries.answer: The main risks are mechanical injury from woodworking machines such as saws and milling equipment, health damage from long-term exposure to wood dust and noise, whole-batch scrap from layout or cutting deviations, finished-product failure from weak joints and assembly, contact risk from adhesives and coating materials, and changing processes beyond equipment authorization; control depends on standard inspection and use of equipment and tooling, guarding and dust and noise control, first-article verification and sampling inspection, controlling fit and fastening per process, ventilation and protection for chemicals, and clear authorization and shutdown escalation procedures.
entries.question: What risks does this job most require you to watch out for in advance?

entries.answer: Fit signals are being able to read drawings and lay out as required, being able to use hand and power tools steadily in a dusty and noisy environment, and being able to stop the machine and report first when a dimension is out of tolerance or equipment is abnormal; having done small wood projects at home is not enough to prove competence — what matters is whether there is reviewable machining precision, first-article verification records, and safe operating habits.
entries.question: How do you judge whether this job suits you?

entries.answer: Material estimating, layout and material optimization, drafting machining programs, summarizing inspection and equipment-check records, and comparing process parameters can be assisted; dimensional and fit judgments, joint and assembly quality, surface-preparation prep, and equipment guarding and shutdown decisions are still checked and owned by the workers.
entries.question: Which steps will AI and automation change?

entries.answer: Dimensional and tolerance judgments, joint and fit conclusions, confirmation of assembly solidity, first-article verification and sampling inspection determinations, equipment guarding status and whether shutdown is required, and whether a material substitution is acceptable must all be completed and documented by an authorized person.
entries.question: Which steps must keep human inspection?

entries.answer: Education and training thresholds must be checked separately (O*NET classifies it as Job Zone 1-2, usually requiring a high school diploma or equivalent, with on-the-job training from a few days to a year), along with equipment operating authorization and training, the scope of responsibility for drawings and tolerances, dust and noise protection measures, and whether you are responsible for sample making and first-article verification; this occupation usually has no uniform individual license.

entries.answer: The O*NET work context shows shop work dominated by long periods of standing: 99% stand continuously or almost continuously, 95% use their hands continuously or almost continuously, 40% are exposed daily to minor burns, cuts, bites, or stings, 25% are exposed to hazardous conditions every day, and 65% wear common protective or safety equipment every day; the main demands come from dust and noise exposure, repetitive motion, and moving lumber.

entries.answer: 96% have a regular work schedule and 27% work more than 40 hours per week; rush-order periods and delivery milestones are concentrated overtime periods; the work style is mainly shop machining and assembly, gauge verification, equipment checks, and written records.

subject.name: Cabinetmakers and Bench Carpenters
subject.summary: This page's entry corresponds to cabinetmakers and bench carpenters (O*NET-SOC 51-7011.00): cutting, shaping, and assembling wooden articles, or setting up and operating woodworking machines such as power saws, jointers, and mortisers to surface, cut, or shape lumber — measuring and laying out to drawings, truing joints, drilling, assembly and reinforcement, hardware installation, verifying dimensions and fit, and matching materials by color and grain; the work is mainly shop work with long periods of standing (99% stand continuously, 95% use their hands continuously, 40% are exposed daily to minor cuts, 65% wear common protective equipment every day), and its responsibility does not equal structural design approval, nor does it replace responsibility for equipment safety management and on-site installation plans.
